>> Exposed organs - cover with wet sterile dressings (do not attempt to push organs back in)
>> Open chest wound with air leak - occlusive dressing or vented chest seal

_Advance Emergency Medical Technician_

_Paramedic_

*RHONCHI:* Obstruction in lower airway, usually caused by excess mucus in rhonchi. Associated with respiratory infections and pnuemonia.
*DIMINISHED:* Cause should be determined by other signs/symptoms, usually associated with developing pnuemo/hemothorax. Can also be associated with pnuemonia.

When driving without lights or sirens (non-emergent), units must follow all regular road laws - including speed limits, adhering to intersections and other policies. The main changes when responding *with* sirens are:
>> Units may drive 15mph over the area's designated speed limit.
>> *EXERCISE CAUTION* at intersections, slowing down enough to a rate that allows you to safely ensure the intersection is clear before moving through.
>> Lights and sirens must be activated at least 50 feet before performing a U-TURN.
>> If needing to occupy the incorrect lane of travel, remember the oncoming traffic *does* have right of way. Revert back to the correct lane as soon as it is safe to do so.

> High Visibility Vests must be worn on all scenes that are on or near the road.
> If medical personnel come across a patient while enroute to the scene, they now have legal care of that patient. Metro should be notified so they can redivert. (( Exemption occurs if the new patient is a corpse. ))
> If personnel are involved in any form of incident: stop, notify Metro of location and any additional resources. Do not move yourself unless you feel capable of doing so. *DO NOT LEAVE THE SCENE UNTIL CLEARED BY LAW ENFORCEMENT, EVEN IF YOU HAVE A PATIENT AT THE TIME OF THE INCIDENT.* Page for an EMS Supervisor and file an Incident Report (( Forums -> EMS )) within 48 hours.
> Emergency driving privileges may be revoked by EMS/ETB Command.

> Parking is an acquired skill that you will pick up over time, however there are some basic considerations: 
>> Never reverse onto a scene.
>> If your scene is in the road and Law Enforcement have not blocked the road off, your Ambulance should be used to do so by parking it at a 45 degree angle to the left in the lane of which traffic is flowing.
>> If your scene has already been blocked off (if required), you are advised to park at the front of the scene.
>> In the event where neither option is feasible, keep the following in mind: park in a place that does not endanger you, your crew or your patient. It should allow for an easy, swift exit and should not compromise the scene in any other way.

","id":"proto-1763717348859","name":"Emergency Vehicle Protocols"},{"category":"[1] Introduction, Legalities & Guides","content":"*SCOPE OF PRACTICE:* Providers must stick to their designated, legal scope, as defined by their active license. AEMT/Paramedic Interns may *only* practice AEMT+ skills on the field when supervised by their respective Education Officer.

*MEDICAL CONTROL:* can be contacted via METRO if unsure on patient treatment or if advised by the County Protocols. 

*DUTY TO ACT:* when on duty as a first responder, you have a legal obligation to stop and render aid. If you are enroute to an active call and come across somebody in need of help, this is the same - in which case, notify METRO and have them redivert another Ambulance to your original call (( Exemption occurs if the patient is in the corpse pose. ))

*HEALTH INSURANCE PORTABILITY AND ACCOUNTABILITY ACT (HIPAA):* patient confidentiality. Identifying information (i.e names, medical history/records, address or other locations) should only be shared during handover to others *involved in that person's care* (i.e ER staff, a Paramedic taking over the patient's care). _Never_ state patient names over the radio. *Information can only be shared with Law Enforcement if they have a valid warrant, or if the patient is involved in a crime such as homicide, animal abuse, child or domestic abuse etc.* 

*Patient Refusal/Against Medical Advice:* patients must fit the Competence -> Capacity -> Informed Refusal criteria to legally refuse care. Law Enforcement should ideally already be on scene for patients who are a risk to themselves or others. *Do not chase after a patient if they run off, we do not have the legal right to detain.* Ensure all refusals are witnessed and signed via the electronic form. 

>> *CCI CRITERIA: * patient must be over 18 (parent or legal guardian can sign unless PT legally imancipated), patient must be alert and orientated by four (AxO4 - knows where they are, when it is, who they are and what has happened), patient must *not* be an active threat to self or others, patient must not be mentally altered in any form (i.e high, intoxicated, confused, disorientated), patient must be able to communicate fully with the provider (i.e no language barrier), patient must be provided and understand the risks of refusing care
>> *SUSPECTS MAY LEGALLY REFUSE TREATMENT IF THEY MEET THE ABOVE CRITERIA, BUT CANNOT REFUSE TRANSPORT TO A MEDICAL FACILITY. LAW ENFORCEMENT SHOULD REMAIN PRESENT AT ALL TIME WITH ANY PATIENTS WHO ARE CUFFED OR A POSSIBLE RISK.* 

*PHARMALOGICAL LEGALITIES:* acquire (implied if not meeting CCI criteria) consent prior to giving medication, assess medical history and vitals prior *_when_* possible and appropriate. Ensure: right patient, right route, right medication, right dose, right time (five rights of medication). 

","id":"proto-1763717138102","name":"Legalities"},{"category":"[1] Introduction, Legalities & Guides","content":"(( We understand that medical roleplay can seem complex at times, especially if you are dealing with folk who are using specific terminology and information that you are unsure of. We highly encourage the usage of any resources you have available to you - whether it be PM'ing the player if you are unsure, asking in faction chat, Discord, etc. 

The more you practice, the more you will get used to it and the more you will learn. 90% of us start out as beginners and do not have any form of IRL experience or training, just a passion for medical roleplay! Do not be afraid to ask questions and do your own research in your own time. Your roleplay does not have to be overly specific or in depth. Put an emphasis on communicating IC'ly with your patient where able, make it engaging for everyone involved. Don't be afraid to explore what sort of an EMT your character is. Some may crack jokes with patients, some may be a bit less talkative with patients and come across as solely focused on their work! 

Here are some common abbreviations and terms used in medical roleplay:

*AOx1/2/3/4:* Alert and Orientated by X. A patient will score one point for each aspect they are able to answer: who they are, where they are, what happened and when it is.
*LOC:* Level of Consciousness, sometimes Loss of Consciousness
*GCS:* Glascow Coma Scale - you can find out more about the scale at https://www.glasgowcomascale.org
*WNL/WNR:* Within Normal Limits/Within Normal Range, often used for vitals
*Tachy/Brady/Hyper/Hypo X:* _Tachy is fast, brady is slow. Hyper is high and hypo is low!_ Usually follows a secondary term such as cardic (heart rate), pneaic (breathing rate), glycemic (blood sugar), thermic (body temperature. i.e Tachycardia (fast heart rate), bradypnea (slow breathing rate), hyperglycemic (high blood sugar), hypoxic (low oxygen saturation).
*PERRL:* Pupils are Equal, Round and Responsive to Light (normal pupillary response, non-indicative of severe head trauma)
*TPX*: Tension Pnuemothorax
*BPM*: Beats per Minute, sometimes Breaths per Minute when addressing respirations
*RR*: Respiratory (breathing) rate
*SPO2/O2:* Oxygen Saturation/Oxygen Levels
*BP:* Blood Pressure
*PPE/BSI:* Personal Protective Equipment/Body Substance Isolation
*51-50:* Likely Behavioural Emergency (i.e Mental Health Crisis, Psychosis)
*AED:* Automated External Defibrillator
*AVPU:* Used during response assessment: Alert, Verbal Stimuli, Pain Stimuli, Unresponsive
*BGL:* Blood Glucose Level(s)
*C-SPINE:* Cervical-Spine (neck and back)
*SoB:* Shortness of Breath
*GI:* Gastrointestinal 
*IB:* Internal Bleeding
*MCI:* Mass Casualty Incident
*TBI:* Traumatic Brain Injury

","id":"proto-1763728359713","name":"Miscellaneous Information + Tips"},{"category":"[1] Introduction, Legalities & Guides","content":"Radio communications should be kept concise and to the point. Any unit updates or requests should directly go through METRO. Avoid using unnecessary detail. A few examples of sufficient radio transmissions:
> "Medic 801, available on the radio."
> "Medic 801, clearing from Del Perro - patient deceased, available on the radio."
> "Medic 801, handover complete, clearing from Pillbox - unavailable."
> "Medic 801, in service and conditionally available."
> "Medic 801, Metro, requesting ALS to Carson and Brogue - patient is seizing."
> "Medic 801, Metro, advise patient is in cardiac arrest. Starting CPR at 18:02, no further units needed at this time." 

Pillbox Units should *NOT* be self-dispatching to scenes _unless_ Fire Metro has explicitly stated we can self-dispatch _*or*_ Metro services are not online (( FD are not on duty )). Police and Sheriff's can request Ambulance units through the departmental radio - however, again, these requests should be left for METRO to handle unless they are not in service. 

Remember to update the CAD when giving radio status updates (( /fcad )).

METRO = Main dispatch channel, used for unit status updates and requests
TAC 1/TAC 2 = Incident specific channels assigned by METRO during larger scale incidents
PHMC BASE = primary PHMC radio, used for handovers and internal department communication

*HANDOVERS AND ENCODES* Encodes are done over the PHMC frequency to aler the ER of incoming patients. This is usually a brief run down of the key points concerning the patient's condition. Handovers are done in-person with the receiving ER staff, and are usually more thorough.

> ENCODES
>> Patient names should never be mentioned on the radio.
>> Transmissions are usually brief and cover the key issues of the patient.
>> Remember *DMIST*: Demographics, Mechanism of Injury/Illness, Injuries, Signs/Symptoms & Treatment
>> *EXAMPLE*: Medic 801, BLS alert. Enroute with an adult male, K9 bite. Alert and responsive. All vitals are stable, bleeding controlled on scene. ETA 4 minutes. 
>> *EXAMPLE*: Medic 801, trauma alert. Enroute with a thirty year old female with multiple gunshot wounds to the abdomen. Decreasing level of consciousness - blood pressure is low, oxygen saturation steady on high flow oxygen. Bleeding controlled on scene. ETA 2."
>> *EXAMPLE*: Medic 801, trauma alert. Enroute with a paediatric male, motor vehicle vs. pedestrian. Alert and orientated by two. Chief complaint of neck and abdominal pain. All vitals within normal range. Pupils PERRL, C-SPINE precautions in place, low flow oxygen provided. ETA 10.

> HANDOVER
>> Usually more thorough, delves into the patient's history and mechanism of injury a bit more.
>> Opportunity to give ER staff patient's identifying details (i.e medical history, name).
>> Always ask the receiving staff whether they have any questions or need anything.
>> *EXAMPLE (TRAUMA):* This is Jack, unknown age. Struck by a vehicle at high speeds approximately 10 minutes ago. Unresponsive on scene initially, he's now awake but isn't orientated, no memory of what happened. Uncombative. Complaining of strong pain on the right side of his abdomen, no bruising but area is tender on palpation. Closed fracture identified to the right left and lower left arm. Vitals have remained steady through transport. Any questions?
>> *EXAMPLE (MEDICAL):* This is Millie Johnson, 32 years old. Initially called for general weakness - on arrival, she was responsive to EMS crews but disorientated to time and place. Her husband's stated she's been feeling unwell for a couple of days and hasn't been eating, blood sugars were low when we checked so we've given her some oral glucose. Her temperature is pretty high, heart rate and blood pressure are elevated as well. Oxygen levels were low on room air so we've got her on a NRB. Husband states she has no medical conditions but that she has allergies to penicillin and soy. Meets current SEPSIS criteria at this time."

Handovers and encodes will vary greatly depending on if there has been BLS vs. ALS intervention, and on how stable the patient is.","id":"proto-1763717317031","name":"Radio Procedures + Encodes"},{"category":"[1] Introduction, Legalities & Guides","content":"(( Welcome to the internal version of the Los Santos County Emergency Medical Services protocols. The _official_ version of these protocols can be found here: https://lsfd.gta.world/LSCC/protocols. These protocols have been tailored slightly for our faction directly, with the main goal of localizing all of our information and making procedures simpler to understand.

*Always* start with the General Patient Assessment under Section 2. From there, figure out what other protocols may apply to your patient. For example, let's say you find Wheezing during your primary assessment - you would then navigate to Section II for further information. Or, if at any point, your patient's heart stops beating (cardiac arrest), you would go to the relevant Cardiac Arrest protocol. 

*START FROM THE TOP, WORK YOUR WAY DOWN AND STICK TO YOUR SCOPE*. If you are an EMT, you only need to worry about the instructions listed under "Emergency Medical Technician" in that specific protocol. If you are a Paramedic, you will need to also consider the scope instructions underneath you and exercise these through on-scene delegation. 

Our protocols are also equipped with a myriad of highlights that can be clicked on. These further explain certain procedures and also give you important information when it comes to different medications - such as when *_NOT_* to give them. Try not to over-think medical roleplay too much and remember that you have resources available to you if you are ever stuck.

For any bugs, errors or queries regarding this site, please contact either Alyson Frost (fr0stydev) or Ellie Ohara (itzmisuzu) on Discord. )) ","id":"proto-1763717091624","name":"Introduction"}]}]}

1) How do I request an autopsy report and/or a death certificate?
Autopsies and death certificates can aid in various situations, especially whenever the cause of death plays a vital role in. Our professionals attempt to handle each and every request in a timely manner. However, given the fact that the effort of documentation is immense, a request fee is associated along with it. Upon its payment, the report or certificate will be sent to you directly.


2) Is there a fee associated with the request process?
Yes, there is a $2,000 fee associated with the request. This fee covers administrative costs related to processing and maintaining your requested report/certificate securely within our systems. It ensures the continued improvement of our services, maintaining the highest standards in healthcare data management.


3) How do I pay the $2,000 request fee?
To pay your $2,000 request fee, please log into the banking website and navigate to the "Payment" section. Select your preferred payment method (e.g., credit card, debit card), insert our routing number (020000062), enter the required payment details, review the transaction, and confirm your payment. (( Type /transfer 2000 020000062 ))
